rules.statement: Make a ValueTask-returning wait method non-async when it often finishes synchronously: return ValueTask.CompletedTask if the underlying task has already completed, and otherwise return new ValueTask(task.WaitAsync(cancellationToken)).
rules.why: An async method runs and allocates a state machine even in the common case where the wait is already over.
rules.check: Look for `async ValueTask` methods whose only await is a task that is frequently already complete (e.g. a `Task.CompletedTask` returned when the resource is free) with no fast path.

rules.statement: Don't report a foreach over an interface-typed collection for enumerator allocation when the loop runs on a path that isn't per-request (for example, once per session end) or when the empty case iterates a shared empty array.
rules.why: The allocation-free loop rule targets per-request paths, and .NET hands out a cached enumerator for an empty array, so the empty case allocates nothing.
rules.check: Before reporting, check how often the loop runs (per request or per lifecycle event) and whether an empty result is the shared Array.Empty instance.

rules.statement: On read paths that may return an empty collection, use a shared empty instance (such as Array.Empty<T>() or a `[]` collection expression typed as IEnumerable<T> or IReadOnlyList<T>) instead of allocating a new empty List<T> each time.
rules.why: Each read of an empty result otherwise allocates a list it doesn't need.
rules.check: Look for `new List<T>()`, or a `[]` assigned to a List<T>-typed target, produced for an empty result on frequently called read, watch or notification paths.

rules.statement: Don't report a method call inside an object initializer's property assignment as a violation of the rule against nesting a call inside another call's arguments.
rules.why: A property assignment in an initializer isn't an argument, and it reads as the member's value. No convention covers calls in initializers.
rules.check: Before reporting a nested call, confirm that the inner call really is an argument to another call, not the value in an initializer assignment.

rules.statement: In a test project, don't ask to split a test that drives one behavior and asserts more than one of its effects (such as the return value and the resulting state), even when its name joins them with 'And'.
rules.why: The test conventions ask for one behavior per test, not one assertion per test.
rules.check: Before reporting, decide whether the test performs one action whose several effects it asserts (acceptable) or performs a second, separate action and asserts on that.

rules.statement: In a test project, when a test verifies its named behavior and then performs a further action and asserts on that, move the further action and its assertions into a separate, named test.
rules.why: Otherwise a failure in either half points at the whole test, and the test's name describes only the first behavior.
rules.check: Look for tests that act again (publish, call or advance) after the assertions for the behavior in their name, and then assert on that second action.

rules.statement: In a test project, declare each IDisposable the test creates (such as an object that owns a timer) with `using var`, and have helpers take the disposable as a parameter rather than create it, so that the test owns and disposes it.
rules.why: Undisposed objects leave live resources such as timers behind instead of releasing them deterministically.
rules.check: Look for `var x = new SomeDisposable(...)` in tests without `using`, and for helper methods that create a disposable internally that no caller disposes.

rules.statement: Replace an unexplained hard-coded duration with a named constant whose documentation says why that value was chosen (for example, that it only has to outlive the call).
rules.why: Otherwise readers have to work out why that particular value is used.
rules.check: Look for inline literals such as `TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)` whose purpose isn't clear from context.
